[PAPER_0020, relevance_score=0.210] Specifically, encoding certainty implies that (nearly) equivalent stimuli in terms of their emotional intensity would also be encoded nearly equivalently in terms of felt intensities, that is, would generate nearly equivalent drift rates and a tiny SV. The fact that the stimuli were not coded equivalently implies uncertainty. We therefore predicted that, if Weber's law holds for (un)pleasant feelings, an increase in normative intensity (across the six homogeneous valence categories) would be associated with increased encoding uncertainty and in turn with an increase in SV.

[PAPER_0030, relevance_score=0.341] Our two main predictions were as follows: (P1) DR and normative ratings would monotonically covary, showing that the drift rate provides a scale for emotion intensity, and given that drift rate has a unit and a zero point, the result would show that it provides a ratio scale for measuring emotional intensity. Additionally, (P2) SV would increase with the stimulus's emotional intensity, thus conforming to the hypothesis that emotions behave like most other sensations and approximately obey Weber's law.

[PAPER_0063, relevance_score=0.347] Testing P1

Once we established the legitimacy of the LBA as a model of the current results, we could move to testing the core predictions. For M-P, we found that as valence became less negative and more positive, DR increased (BF10 = 4.943e + 81; Figure 5a). For M-N, we found that as valence became less negative and more positive, the DR decreased (BF10 = 1.327e + 76; Figure 5a).

An alternative hypothesis is that emotion resembles "action" related perception, and as such does not obey Weber's Law.

[PREREG_0028, relevance_score=0.335] This method will be used by us in the analyses of few of our hypothesis.

To test our hypothesis that emotional awareness obeys Weber's law, we first need to show that the LBA model is suitable to find evidence to Weber's law even for physical stimuli. We thus intend to show that the LBA model can detect Weber's law for the perception of circle size. We term the related hypothesis "tool-validity hypothesis" (TVH) to mark the fact that it is not a core hypothesis.

[PREREG_0032, relevance_score=0.346] We than re-run the model with both new data sets, and examined whether the percentage of subjects to fit one model compared to the other model remain almost the same. If the percentage will remain quite like the percentages of the first analysis, we can conclude that the differences between both models are not coincidental.

If our hypothesis is not supported by the data, we have two options: First, the LBA model is not suitable to express Weber's law. The second option is that something in the experimental procedure went wrong, then we can fix it and try again.

[PREREG_0033, relevance_score=0.348] Importantly, until (or whether) the tool-validity hypothesis is supported is a pre-requisite for testing the core hypothesis which is described next.

In order to test our core hypothesis (that emotional awareness obey Weber's law), we will compare between several alternative models which are strictly analogous to the models we have described above, except for being applied to (un) pleasantness reports.

The circle task is used for two purposes: (1) to create a validated reference-point to the emotional and gamble tasks.

[PREREG_0034, relevance_score=0.421] (2) To function as a disguise (subjects will be led to believe that we are examining whether emotional stimulation/ gamble outcomes affect perception of circles area). In order to create a validated reference-point, we will use the method of model comparison as described above, and apply it on the difference between tasks (circle, emotional). We expect to find that the model that will show to be superior to the other models, is the model that allows the SP parameter to vary between tasks. This hypothesis is in accordance with previous work conducted in our lab (Givon et al., 2019).

Participants were recruited through Ben Gurion University's online system. We collected data from 34 participants, of whom 29 were women. Most participants were undergraduate students in their early 20s. All the participants reported having intact/corrected vision. In addition, given the highly aversive nature of some stimuli, we informed the participants that the study is unsuitable for people who suffer from depression, phobia, or anxiety.

[PAPER_0036, relevance_score=0.337] We additionally asked the candidate participants to fill out a depression questionnaire, and only participants whose scores fell within the nonpathological range took part in the experiment. All participants received course credit or monetary gain for their participation.

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.327] The Perceptual Task

In trials of the perceptual task (Figure 2b), participants were introduced to a standard circle with a fixed-size diameter (225 pixels), and their task was to determine whether the next circle presented to them was larger or smaller than the standard circle. There were four circles that were larger than the standard circle and four that were smaller than it. Each circle area was 5% larger/smaller than its previous circle in the series.

Since this experiment was conducted during COVID-19, participants performed the experiment using their own personal laptop at their own homes.

Follow-up analyses

In this study we will use a method of model comparison to test some of our hypothesis. The fundamental idea in this method is to fit several different LBA models, and to decide which model fits the data best. To do so, we will create the null model (M1) with all its parameters set to be equal across different levels of the dependent variable in question.

[PREREG_0026, relevance_score=0.505] Then, we will create five more models (M2-M6), which in every one of those models a different parameter will set as a function of the dependent variable. The null model will serve as a comparison model to the other models.

Because hierarchical modeling is a time-consuming process, we will use hierarchical modeling only for our main hypotheses. In addition, in order to interpret the data obtained from the hierarchical analysis, the Gelman-Robin index for each individual and for all subjects together must be less than 1.1.

[PREREG_0027, relevance_score=0.433] If we won't meet this requirement, or if the hypotheses under examination is not a main hypothesis, we will use simpler methods for estimating the model parameters. The simpler method treats the data as if they came from "one big subject". This approach is based on maximum likelihood estimation, and issues BIC values for comparative model fit assessment. This method will conduct using 'rtdists' or 'glba' R packages. Any model that will have a significant smaller DIC or BIC then M1, will account as a model that fit the data the best.

We expect to find that the model that will show to be superior to the other models, is the model that allows the SP parameter to vary between tasks. This hypothesis is in accordance with previous work conducted in our lab (Givon et al., 2019).

[PAPER_0032, relevance_score=0.290] Method

Transparency and Openness

We report in the main text (and online supplemental materials ) how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study. All data and R codes are available at https://osf.io/m6j93/. Data cleaning, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, linear trend analysis, and data visualization were conducted using R (R Core Team, 2020), while Bayesian repeated-measures analysis of variance was conducted using JASP (JASP Team, 2020).

[PAPER_0045, relevance_score=0.262] Model Fitting

For modeling purposes, we defined correct and wrong emotion reports according to adherence to norms, an assumption justified by the fact that aberrant emotion reports have been shown to be processed similarly to aberrant perceptual decisions-that is, errors (Givon et al., 2022), most importantly in terms of aberrant RT distributions being relatively more right skewed but also in terms of speed-accuracy trade-off, post-error slowing, and electroencephalogram error-related negativity.

[PAPER_0048, relevance_score=0.241] Specifically, in M-P, DR and SV of "pleasant" were free parameters. These include the parameters of the normative "pleasant" responses to normatively positive stimuli, a pair of DR and SV parameters for each one of the three intensity levels ~6, ~7, and ~8. It also included the parameters representing the accumulator generating normatively aberrant "pleasant" responses to normatively negative stimuli (intensity levels ~2, ~3, ~4). The rest of the parameters were fixed to reduce model complexity, thereby improving parameter estimation.
